title: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
summary: Other countries have rerouted trade in response to his first tariff salvo, now they are looking beyond Trump's tenure.
text:
Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
- Published
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.
Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.
"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.
Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.
The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.
Still, the USA is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.
The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.
It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.
The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".
The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

title: In a fertility advance, engineered molecular glue stabilizes chromosomes in aging eggs
summary: Researchers engineered a protein system capable of restoring normal chromosome connections in aging mouse eggs, raising hopes of one day improving IVF outcomes
text:
Around the world, people are increasingly choosing to have babies later in life for reasons both social and economic. As they get older though, they face a mounting biological challenge: genetic errors caused by chromosomes failing to separate correctly. This phenomenon, known as aneuploidy, is the leading cause of age-related infertility, failed in-vitro fertilization (IVF) cycles, and miscarriage, and it increases dramatically around the age of 40. Studies have shown that between 50% and 80% of embryos from women in their 40s carry chromosomal abnormalities.
One of the main drivers of aneuploidy is the loss of a protein complex called cohesin, which acts like a molecular glue holding chromosomes together. In a new study, researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences in Göttingen, Germany, engineered a novel protein system capable of restoring normal chromosome connections in aging mouse eggs. The study, published Thursday in Science, raises the possibility of one day developing such a system into a treatment that could reduce aneuploidy in human eggs used for IVF.
“There is still work ahead, but their proof of concept was highly successful,” said Rajiv McCoy, a biologist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the work. McCoy’s lab is focused on pregnancy loss, the leading cause of which is aneuploidy. It is estimated that about half of all human conceptions are lost before birth, including the roughly 15% of known pregnancies that end in miscarriage. Technologies that could reduce the odds of miscarriage and expand women’s biological reproductive windows by addressing aneuploidy would have far-reaching consequences for the IVF industry and for society at large. “The stakes are very high,” McCoy said.
When a cell prepares to divide, its chromosomes replicate, forming two copies, or sister chromatids, that are all lined up and organized by a cellular winch system known as the spindle. Within the spindle, the sister chromatids are tethered to each other by cohesin — its ring-like structure traps DNA from both sisters inside it. In most cells, cohesin only has to do this work for a few hours before other enzymes cleave it apart, freeing the chromatids to separate into two new cells. But in oocytes, cohesin has to keep this bond going for decades.
That’s because female babies are born with all the oocytes they will ever have. And already at birth, those 1 to 2 million immature egg cells have begun to divide, and the cohesin’s job is only finished when fertilization occurs. That triggers the end of the division process called meiosis in which the egg cells eject half their genetic material so they can fuse with sperm to make an embryo.
Over all that time, the cohesin molecule doesn’t seem to be reloaded, said Melina Schuh, a director at the Max Planck Institute who led the new work.

title: U.S. Judge rules FCC violated ABC's free speech rights to please Trump
summary: A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration from moving to review all local broadcast licenses held by ABC. The stations air in six of the largest U.S. markets.
text:
U.S. Judge rules FCC violated ABC's free speech rights to please Trump
U.S. judge rules FCC violated ABC’s free speech rights to please Trump
A federal judge has blocked President Trump and his administration from taking action to challenge the ABC television network's broadcast licenses, finding it to be an unconstitutional punishment for satire, commentary and news coverage that Trump doesn't like.
In her preliminary injunction filed Wednesday, U.S. District Court Judge Loren AliKhan found that the federal agency's early reviews represented retaliation for speech the Trump administration resented.
Such perceived offenses included late-night host Jimmy Kimmel's jabs at the president, the critical remarks of hosts on the chat show The View, and the moderation of a presidential debate in September 2024.
ABC and its corporate parent, the Walt Disney Co., serve six of the 10 largest markets in the U.S., including New York, Los Angeles, and Houston. They contribute significantly to the network's bottom line.
"Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face -- loss of their broadcast licenses -- the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness," Judge AliKhan wrote.
She rejected the Trump administration's motion to dismiss the lawsuit from ABC and Disney challenging the review of the local licenses. Usually the licenses last eight years and are up for review on a staggered basis. They are rarely taken away.
In her ruling, AliKhan relied heavily on public statements and social media postings in which Trump attacked ABC and Disney, as well as posts by Trump's pick as the chair of the Federal Communications Commission, Brendan Carr.
"What started in 2020 as questions about how ABC 'can keep getting a license' if it 'report[s] fake news,' ... has crescendoed into repeated calls for the Commission to strip ABC's broadcast licenses for their editorial decisions," she wrote. "The court counts eleven such calls made by President Trump over the past two years -- the most recent being in July 2026."
And the judge cited the administration's "tangible steps toward enforcing President Trump and Commissioner Carr's repeated threats to strip the Plaintiff Stations of their licenses."
"Chairman Carr has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders," Judge AliKhan wrote.
Carr did not respond to NPR's request for comment Wednesday evening.
ABC hailed the ruling in a statement as "an important victory for the First Amendment."
Among the targets of ire from Trump and Carr was ABC's decision not to broadcast Trump's July 2026 Oval Office address on its television network. ABC's legal team said the network streamed it on its digital news service, but would not have done so absent the political pressure from the FCC.

title: When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered
summary: Why is Poundland closing down, and what will happen to staff and suppliers?
text:
When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered
- Published
Poundland has collapsed into administration, leaving the jobs of its 11,000 staff in doubt in the run-up to Christmas.
The company has appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer, with questions remaining about the future of the company.
1. When will Poundland shops close?
This is the question that is most difficult to answer.
Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in the process of selling it.
Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, which is the more likely outcome.
When Poundland was still a going concern, Irish property firm Martin Property Group made an offer for it. But a source said the group was now "unlikely" to make a fresh bid due to "irreparable harm" to the brand from the administration process.
Before the collapse, Fortress, which owns rival budget chain Poundstretcher, was interested in buying about 200 of the stores, and wanted to keep those trading under the Poundland brand.
But Fortress's position at the moment is unclear. The BBC understands it is considering selling Poundstretcher, a move first reported by Bloomberg.
A decision on Poundstretcher could come before the end of this week. However, Fortress has declined to comment.
2. Why is Poundland closing down?
That depends on who you ask.
When the chain was sold by Pepco last year for £1 it was struggling. It suffered a £68m loss that year.
Poundland's managing director Barry Williams said Poundland had been seeing a "strong recovery" and recorded a profit by one measure in the first nine months of this year.
Poundland's management paint a picture of a retailer that was turning a corner until the owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, pulled the plug on funding for day-to-day expenses such as buying stock.
The Usdaw union, which represents shopworkers, claim the owners forced Poundland into administration.
Labour MP Antonia Bance said she was "pretty appalled" by the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the past few weeks, and that it was going to make much bigger profits by breaking up the business rather than by keeping it going.
However, Gordon Brothers insisted the business was only turning a profit on paper, and had missed budget forecasts.
A spokeswoman said while the management team had made £100m in cost reductions, the business had moved from a £70m loss to "around break-even".
"Break-even is different from generating the cash needed to buy stock, invest, and withstand increasing economic pressures," the spokeswoman said. "A few good weeks do not make a turnaround."
Poundland repeatedly missed budget targets over the year, the spokeswoman added.
Gordon Brothers was concerned that as inflation goes up next year, those pressures would have helped to make the business unviable, it said.

title: STAT+: The grueling struggle to find a primary care doctor in the ‘medical capital’ of America
summary: Boston is supposed to be the medical capital of America. Yet many don’t have primary care access, hurting their ability to get treatments, screenings, and medical advice.
text:
I was three days into calling doctors’ offices, trying to get a primary care appointment. Over and over, I sat on hold, only to hear I’d have to wait weeks or months. It was mind numbing.
Then I reached a voicemail greeting that sounded about as despondent as I felt.
“We’ve received an extremely high volume of messages due to multiple providers in our area retiring or leaving their practice very recently,” the woman’s voice said with a hint of exasperation, “so please understand it may take longer than normal to receive a return call back.”

title: Medicare Open Enrollment: Here’s What’s Changing, and What Mistakes To Avoid
summary: Medicare’s zero-premium drug plans are disappearing, millions are losing their plans, and the average prescription drug plan premium could rise 50% if you stay put. Here’s what to check.
text:
Medicare Open Enrollment: Here’s What’s Changing, and What Mistakes To Avoid
Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people. The coverage choices are complex and often consequential.
Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn’t one plan. It’s more like a build-your-own-insurance menu.
Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there’s no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn’t cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services.
As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D, the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.
This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums.
“People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs,” said David Lipschutz, a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.
The Hassle Saves Money
Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It’s a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can’t find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projects that the average Part D premium will increase less than $1 a month for a standalone prescription drug plan, describing the market as stable. But that average doesn’t tell the whole story. An analysis by KFF, the health policy research nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, found that enrollees who stay in their prescription drug plan will see a 50% increase on average, from $34 to $51. About 10.4 million people could pay higher premiums, not including higher deductibles and coinsurance costs.

title: Why Medicare’s 2027 physician pay changes worry some specialists
summary: Cuts to Medicare physician payment rates for certain same-day services could impact some specialists more than others.
text:
Podiatrist Heather McGuire always wanted to serve in a clinic in her hometown of Ventura, Calif. Fifteen years after she opened her practice, she is realizing her dream in the community that raised her, treating suburbanites and agricultural workers with diabetes on Medicare.
But McGuire believes that dream may be ending.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ recent update to how Medicare pays physicians cut the payment rate for certain services provided on the same day by 20% when it’s provided by the same physician or practice. McGuire’s practice already operates on extremely thin margins, and she recently shelved a plan to hire another doctor to improve the practice’s exceedingly long wait times.
It could worsen Medicare recipients’ access to specialist care in Ventura, too. Last week, the podiatrist saw a new patient, a woman in her 80s, who waited two and a half months for an appointment to get her heel pain checked out. When the patient arrived, McGuire found that it wasn’t just heel pain. The woman had also developed an ulcer on her other foot during her long appointment wait. Left unchecked, an ulcer in someone with diabetes can lead to amputations.
“I would be paid 20% less for providing potentially lifesaving or limb-saving treatment care for that wound because she also had another complaint at the same visit,” McGuire said.
Podiatrists, dermatologists, and otolaryngologists are among the biggest losers with this change, according to an analysis by the American Medical Association, an advocacy group for physicians. Opponents of the policy, including the AMA, say it will force patients to return for separate appointments, raise out-of-pocket costs, and increase wait times, especially for patients in rural areas who have less access to specialists.
“If you’re running your own small group practice [accepting Medicare patients], can you still financially do that?” said Miranda Franco, a senior policy adviser at the law firm Holland & Knight. “Or are you going to start thinking about, you know, maybe consolidating into a hospital system or private equity to defray some of that financial loss?”
These billing code changes are an attempt to modernize Medicare and reduce administrative burden, a CMS spokesperson said. It is part of the agency’s broader shift away from specialist care and the fee-for-service model, and one of many reimbursement challenges that specialists are contending with.
Not everyone is against the change in payment rates for services rendered on the same day. The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission, a nonpartisan group that advises Congress on Medicare, supports it, saying it will remove redundancies and duplicative payments. The Justice Department has also found multiple instances of providers committing fraud through this billing code.

title: As States Lose OB-GYNs, Some Look To Limit Medical Malpractice Risk
summary: Since 2025, at least four states have enacted laws restricting medical malpractice lawsuits. Patient advocates warn that the laws impose more of a burden on families harmed during childbirth and often pass with little attention.
text:
As States Lose OB-GYNs, Some Look To Limit Medical Malpractice Risk
When Anyssa Zancanella’s water broke during a family vacation near Salt Lake City, she expected better care there than she could get back home in rural Rock Springs, Wyoming, where many patients are flown out for emergency treatment.
Instead, a crisis unfolded. Staff kept raising her doses of Pitocin, a drug that strengthens contractions, while the fetal monitor recorded mounting distress: The baby wasn’t getting enough oxygen. It took nearly 12 hours for the then-19-year-old to get an emergency cesarean section after the monitor showed signs of fetal distress, according to court records.
Azaylee, now 7, was born with brain damage, likely from a reduced supply of oxygen and blood flow during delivery, causing cognitive disabilities, according to her family’s complaint. Last year, a judge found Steward Health Care, a Dallas-based for-profit health system that owned the West Valley City, Utah, hospital at the time, liable for gross medical negligence — and awarded the family $951 million. Steward Health Care did not respond to a request for comment for this article.
Medical malpractice lawsuits against OB-GYNs are common in the U.S. healthcare system — childbirth can carry high risk and serious consequences. As a result, medical malpractice insurance costs for OB-GYNs are higher than for other specialties. Hospital administrators repeatedly cite the costs of those lawsuits and medical liability premiums as a reason to close their labor and delivery units. So, in recent years, state lawmakers began turning to what they say is a solution: tougher limits on malpractice lawsuits.
Since 2025, at least four states, including Oklahoma, have enacted restrictions on medical malpractice suits. Utah added protections shielding physicians’ personal assets. New Mexico capped punitive damages, which punish wrongdoing beyond financial losses, and raised the standard of proof, requiring “clear and convincing” evidence for punitive damages. And Arkansas shortened the window a patient can file those suits after delivery.
The laws often pass with little fanfare, and patient advocates warn they impose more of a burden on families harmed during childbirth, many of whom don’t realize for years that they’ve been survivors of medical malpractice.

Other critics say the actions ignore alternative ways to retain obstetricians, such as addressing abortion bans, which several states pursued in this month’s midterm elections.

title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
summary: Text of the treaties was published this afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
text:
New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
- Published
The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.
The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.
Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.
The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.
The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.
A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released.

- Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost the export of major agricultural commodities.
The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.
Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.
Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."
"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."
A plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.
The treaty text also contains finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. The UK will be invited to attend European Commission meetings and expert groups as an observer, as well as taking part in emergency food security planning.

title: What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
summary: 59% of U.S. shoppers plan to use AI for holiday shopping this weekend, according to the National Retail Federation
text:
What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
Artificial intelligence is here to help with Black Friday.
This weekend, 59% of consumers plan on using AI to support their winter shopping, according to the National Retail Federation.
But AI has proven one way it is not unlike humans: It makes mistakes. The stakes of those hallucinations are much higher when your wallet – and holiday unwrapping memories – are on the line. These tools also become better shoppers when you hand over personal data, which also means giving up more information on your private life to massive tech companies.
Here are some tips – and notes of caution – before using AI as your personal holiday shopper.
Treat AI searches like a conversation with a kid
Traditional online shopping is about search terms and the infinite product scroll. AI is meant to be a conversation.
Unlike shopping on a retail website, AI platforms are designed to look more like texting apps. Prompt bars on these platforms sit on the bottom of the page, inviting a back and forth chat between user and bot about what to buy.
After all, it can be hard to know what keyword to plug in to shop for uncle before the Christmas exchange. AI instead allows for search based on a vibe – like describing that uncle's hobbies and personal style. If a shopper wants to buy a suitcase to support their uncle's European travel dreams, this makes it easier to narrow down the options.
"You can say if that bag is overstuffed, will it fit under the seat on JetBlue?" says Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester who advises retailers and brands on digital commerce strategy, including for AI. "Don't give me the dimensions," she advises, "Tell me if it will suit my use case."
Pfeiffer cautions that even though AI is able to think through these nuanced shopping criteria, it works better with more hand holding.
"It's best if you imagine that it's a young child who will probably misinterpret your request," Pfeiffer said. "You want to be as specific and clear as possible."
AI Agents can shop for you. Be careful what you give them
Newer AI models can do more than talk and brainstorm. They can handle shopping tasks.
If shoppers are, for example, worried about holiday shipments arriving on time, AI can monitor an email inbox in order to track packages, even messaging a late shipper on the shopper's behalf. Beyond just suggesting a gift, agents can do the actual buying (with your money).
These are useful features, but require granting access to sensitive personal data, such as an inbox or credit card. One of the first questions Meta's AI agent platform Muse asks is if the user would like to connect their email and calendar.
Meta says its AI is highly secure. Everyone is assigned their own AI agent and the company promises that information shoppers share with it is kept private. Particularly sensitive information like credit card numbers, they say, are held separately and never viewed directly by the AI.

title: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
summary: The carrier is looking for urgent funding, but will file for bankruptcy without a financial lifeline.
text:
Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
- Published
The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.
The airline said if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.
The airline uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.
Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket.
Flight disruption
One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.
The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.
PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.
In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.
Londoner Fred was due to fly to Cape Town with Norse Atlantic next week for a friend's wedding, but has decided to change his plans.
"Yesterday the exact same flight I was going to get was cancelled, so I was worried" he told the BBC's Your Voice. "I sent an email to Norse and have had nothing back".
He decided to rebook with a different airline, which cost him an extra £1,000.
Another traveller, Claire from Herefordshire, is currently on holiday in South Africa with her daughter.
"We are due to fly home on Sunday and are now looking at a really expensive flight back," she said.
"We have tried contacting Norse but have been given an automated response saying someone will get back to us within three business days."
Advice for passengers
Consumer group Which? advised Norse Atlantic customers to not cancel their flights as the airline has not collapsed. Doing so removes passengers' right to a refund.
Rory Boland, Which? travel editor, said: "If Norse does go bust, whether you get a refund depends on how you booked and paid. If you booked directly with Norse, you may be able to claim a refund via your credit card provider, or possibly your debit card."
Those stuck abroad should contact insurers, while those with package holidays reliant on Norse Atlantic flights should contact their tour operator, he added.
Low-cost, long-haul
Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.
It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.
But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.
Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.
This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly high

text:

title: Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap
summary: Constantly buying new things can be problematic, says journalist Eric Athas, author of the new book "Saying No to New." Here's how to break the cycle and find joy in what you already have.
text:
Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
Buyer beware: Holiday shopping season is here. Is every sale calling your name? Is your virtual shopping cart overflowing?
Before you start buying everything, take note. There's a reason new things get us excited, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New: Why New Things Are Stealing Your Time, Money, and Happiness — and How to Take Back Your Life, published in September. Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible.
That constant consumption of novel possessions — whether they're brand-new, digital, secondhand or even free — can be problematic. "It's hard to be grateful for what you have if you're always on the lookout for something else," he says.
To break the cycle of chasing newness, we need to shop with more intention and find joy in what we already own, Athas says. In a conversation with Life Kit, he explains how. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Why are we so drawn to seeking out new things?
Our brains are programmed to find new things interesting and old things boring.
If you think about our ancient ancestors, it was beneficial [for their survival] to explore new foods to eat and new territory and eventually explore different parts of the world.
There's also research that shows when we encounter something new, we get a little shot of dopamine. You get that feeling of excitement when you first use that new app or try that new video game or bring home a new gizmo for the kitchen.
What are some of the downsides of chasing newness?
New things can steal our happiness. Everyone can relate to the feeling of tearing open that new box or putting on that new outfit. You do feel joy and excitement from that initially.
But science says those feelings can't last. So we have to go out and get something else, and that's where we can get into this cycle of constantly chasing happiness in new things.
These days, it feels particularly hard to focus on what you have. There's so much pressure to buy new things. Why is that?
Everywhere we go, whether that's scrolling our favorite shopping app or browsing the aisle of our favorite store, there are little cues driving our [shopping] decisions. These companies have designs we don't even realize are engineering our choices.
For example, at the checkout page of a website or an app, there might be a countdown clock that says, "Save 25% if you make this purchase in three minutes." That's a tactic meant to whip up anxiety.
The other part of this is that you can buy new things faster than you've ever been able to before. It's all seamless and frictionless.
What can we do to create more friction between ourselves and the new things we want to buy?

title: Millions of people to see average monthly mortgage payments rise by £100
summary: More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated.
text:
Millions of people to see average monthly mortgage payments rise by £100
- Published
More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated, new figures from the the Bank of England show.
About 6.5 million owners are forecast to see their monthly repayment jump by £100 on average when they move onto their next deal by the end of 2029, new data in its Financial Stability Report reveals.
That is more the double the £45-a-month hike that the Bank estimated in its last report in July.
In the shorter term, about one million of those homeowners, who are on mortgage rates below 3% and due to refinance by the end of next year, will see an average £200 increase in their monthly repayments.
For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.
Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals, with the average rates on two and five year fixed mortgages at their highest for about three years.
On Thursday, the average rate on a two-year deal was 5.99%, and at 6% for a five-year deal, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts.
Analysts have described the situation as "brutal" for homeowners coming to the end of their fixed deals.
However, the Bank's report points out that the average £100 increase in monthly repayments was half the rise experienced by those refinancing during 2023 and 2024.
Dawn Fazackerley-King is a Pilates instructor who lives near Ipswich and has previously spoken to the BBC about her struggles with the cost of living.
She was on a five-year fixed deal at 1.4%, which she took out in January 2022. But the mother-of-two is about to refix for two years and the best deal she can find is a 5.69% loan. That will push her costs up by about £200 a month.
She is far from alone, with one million homeowners facing a similar increase often because they are coming off deals that were agreed before interest rates began rising in 2022.
The Bank's report said that households facing higher payments "may need to reduce discretionary spending or draw down savings as higher energy and other essential costs feed through".
Most had savings buffers but lower-income households, including renters, had less wriggle room owing to spending a greater proportion of their income on essentials.
Early in November, the Bank raised the benchmark interest rate, which influences borrowing costs for individuals and businesses, for the first time in more than three years, from 3.75% to 4%.

The numbers could change were mortgage rates to fall, primarily if international economic volatility eased.
Even so, the Bank said around 350,000 were already projected to see monthly mortgage repayments fall when they fixed their next deal within three years.

title: Nvidia's board under fire for handling of CEO's alleged affairs
summary: Even as Jensen Huang has returned to work, Nvidia's board is facing criticism over how it handled the crisis brought on by the CEO's alleged affairs.
text:
Nvidia's board under fire for handling of CEO's alleged affairs
Even as Jensen Huang has returned to work, Nvidia's board is facing criticism over how it handled the crisis brought on by the CEO's alleged affairs.
MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:
How did a board that unanimously decided that its CEO must go decide a few days later to bring him right back? We're talking about Nvidia and its founder, former and now current CEO Jensen Huang. NPR's Andrea Hsu has been gathering reaction to the board's handling of the crisis, and she's with us now to tell us more.
Good morning, Andrea.
ANDREA HSU, BYLINE: Good morning.
MARTIN: OK, so let me just point out here that at an all-hands meeting on Tuesday, Huang apologized for hurting his family and violating the company's code of conduct. That's according to a livestream of the meeting which was viewed by The New York Times. He also reportedly said that President Trump didn't pressure the board into bringing him back. NPR has reached out to Nvidia for confirmation of this, but hasn't heard back. You've been hearing from people who know how boards are meant to operate. What are you hearing from them?
HSU: Yeah. Well, there's been criticism from both those who think Jensen Huang shouldn't have been brought back and also those who think it was the right thing to do. And, Michel, let's remember the role of boards - they exist to make informed and deliberate decisions that are in the best interests of the company and its shareholders. In many instances, they are the only mechanism of accountability for companies and CEOs. And in the case of Nvidia, you know, a lot of people say the board fell short on these duties, and we've asked Nvidia for a response to that, but we haven't heard back on that, either.
MARTIN: Now, recognizing that you're getting a range of opinions there, do these experts have thoughts on what should have happened?
HSU: Yeah. Well, many are saying that the board should have made different choices. Our colleague Shannon Bond spoke with Rob Lalka. He's a professor at Tulane's Freeman School of Business (ph), and he points out that in the last decade, there have been a number of high-profile cases similar to what allegedly happened at Nvidia - you know, a CEO having an affair with an employee. It happened at Intel, McDonald's, Nestle. And Lalka says those boards followed their policies, and those CEOs were out. They decided it had to happen to preserve company values and credibility. ROB LALKA: The board basically went around its entire process that it had set in place for that investigation to put him back into power.
MARTIN: But you also mentioned that there are people who think bringing Huang back was the right thing to do. Say more about that.

title: Opinion: Washington and Beijing are building walls around biotechnology. That’s the wrong approach
summary: “Data show that the U.S.-China contest in biotechnology is not one race but several,” writes Michael S. Kinch.
text:
For more than a decade, my colleagues and I at the Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology have tracked every experimental medicine that enters human testing anywhere in the world. Last December, I wrote in STAT that China had reached parity with the United States in terms of the absolute number of new drugs introduced into clinical trials each year. Starting in 2018, the rate of U.S. contributions began to stagnate. Meanwhile, in 2013, Chinese organizations had introduced about 30 new experimental drugs. A decade later, the number topped 400. And there is no reason to expect the momentum in either country is changing.
Over the past month, both governments have seemingly been moving to wall themselves off. On Oct. 16, Beijing proposed barring foreign acquisition of its companies’ proprietary cell and gene platforms. Within a week, the U.S. Department of the Treasury proposed restrictions that would bar Americans from taking equity stakes, forming joint ventures, or making limited-partner investments in Chinese biotech companies and their equipment suppliers.
The proposals from Beijing and Washington do not impact licensing. American drugmakers can keep licensing Chinese molecules, and Chinese companies may develop new medicines to sell to the U.S. and European companies.
That open door matters more than either wall. Data show that the U.S.-China contest in biotechnology is not one race but several. Restricting investment will not help America win the races it is already losing. The bigger threat to U.S. leadership is not Chinese capital. It is the erosion, at home, of the research enterprise that built America’s lead.
The Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology’s newest analysis, published in September in Drug Discovery Today, emphasizes the importance of these continued engagements. My colleagues and I evaluated the 17,000 new drugs that first entered human trials between 2000 and 2024, separating them into eight different modalities. These ranged from conventional pills to gene therapies. The convergence in the numbers of overall active ingredients that we reported last year turned out to be anything but uniform when looking at the details.
The growth by China was concentrated in a key subset of biologics. By the late 2010s, Chinese sponsors often had introduced more, and more novel, cell therapies annually than American sponsors. By the early 2020s, China had matched or exceeded the U.S. in the introduction of new monoclonal antibodies, a commercially important class of biologic drugs. China took a commanding lead in certain categories of monoclonals, such as multispecific antibodies and drug conjugates.
The U.S. still holds a larger share in two categories: nucleic acid drugs and gene therapy. Dominance in both technologies reflects tools built over decades of Western public and private investment. Examples include lipid nanoparticles that conveyed SARS-CoV2 vaccines, viral vectors, and CRISPR gene editing.

title: Unpacking President Trump's financial stake in Nvidia
summary: NPR's Scott Detrow speaks with Dan Alexander, a senior editor at Forbes and author of a book about President Trump's businesses, about the president's holdings in Nvidia given recent news.
text:
Unpacking President Trump's financial stake in Nvidia
NPR's Scott Detrow speaks with Dan Alexander, a senior editor at Forbes and author of a book about President Trump's businesses, about the president's holdings in Nvidia given recent news.
SCOTT DETROW, HOST:
Let's connect a few things we know about this whole Nvidia situation. One is that President Trump said he convinced Nvidia's board of directors to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. Another is that Trump, or the people who manage his money, have purchased a lot of Nvidia stock since this second term began. One more thing to consider. Nvidia's stock price has roughly tripled over the past three years during the AI investment boom and as Jensen Huang has become a trusted advisor to the Trump White House. So how should we think about all this? We're going to bring in Dan Alexander, a senior editor at Forbes, who oversees coverage of money and politics. He's also an MS NOW contributor. Thanks for coming by.
DAN ALEXANDER: Sure thing. Thank you.
DETROW: Is there a number or a stat that you can cite that best represents President Trump's holdings in Nvidia?
ALEXANDER: I'm going to give you a range, unfortunately.
DETROW: OK.
ALEXANDER: But the latest reporting suggests that the range of his holdings is roughly 5 to $54 million. The stock price is moving a lot each year day.
DETROW: Sure.
ALEXANDER: So that's a number that is big, but also undetermined. And keep in mind that Trump's overall liquid holdings are roughly $2 billion.
DETROW: Yeah.
ALEXANDER: So it's a component of a much larger picture.
DETROW: So this is a large amount of money, incredible wealth for most people. But in the scheme of Donald Trump's holdings, not the biggest asset.
ALEXANDER: Not the biggest asset by a long shot. But that doesn't necessarily mean that he doesn't think about the fact that it's an asset.
DETROW: Yeah.
ALEXANDER: And particularly if it's on the higher end of that range, I mean, you know, $50 million certainly matters to Donald Trump.
